teaser: A quiet Suffolk ford, painted in a London studio to out-shout a wall of rival pictures.
review_notes:
Arrowsmith's price of 250 pounds for The Hay Wain, View on the Stour and a small Yarmouth picture is the commonly cited figure; check.
Willy Lott 'only four nights away in over eighty years' is a traditional story reported by Constable's biographer Leslie.
The wheel-soaking / horse-cooling explanation for the wagon standing in the water is a common suggestion, not documented by Constable.
Delacroix repainting parts of the Massacre at Chios after seeing Constable's pictures is his own later account; widely repeated.
Constable living in Keppel Street, London, in 1821 (not yet Charlotte Street): check.
Protests: Fathers4Justice 2013 (photo stuck on canvas), Just Stop Oil July 2022 (paper image taped over, hands glued to frame).

lesson.text: Picture a tall room in Somerset House, London, in May 1821. Paintings cover the walls from knee height to the ceiling, frame against frame, hundreds of them. This is the Royal Academy's summer exhibition, the one show that could make a British painter's name. A small, quiet landscape hung up there simply vanished.

John Constable had learned that the hard way. So from 1819 he began sending canvases about six feet wide, big enough to hold their ground on that crowded wall. He called them his “six-footers.” This one, the third, measures about 130 by 185 cm (roughly 4 by 6 feet). It was built for a fight.

The odd thing is where he painted it. Not on this riverbank in Suffolk, in eastern England, but in his London house, some 60 miles away, during the winter. He worked from pencil drawings and small oil studies made on the spot years earlier, some of them almost twenty years old.

To get the cart right from that distance, Constable asked a friend's son back in Suffolk, Johnny Dunthorne, to draw a local hay wagon and mail the sketch to London. A “wain” is simply an old word for a farm wagon.

Before the final canvas he did something almost no one else did: he painted a rough version at full size, all six feet of it, just to test the masses of light and dark. That enormous sketch survives in the Victoria and Albert Museum. Then he started again, slower. So who did he put in this remembered place?

lesson.title: Four lives at work
lesson.text: No heroes, no story from a book. Only people doing what they did every summer on the River Stour.

spots.title: The empty wagon
spots.text: Two men ride a wagon with nothing in it. They are on the way out to fetch hay, not bringing it home. The red on the horses' harness is the warmest note in the whole picture.

spots.title: At the water's edge
spots.text: A woman leans from a small landing beside the house, dipping something into the stream. Washing, or fetching water: a daily chore, half lost in shadow.

spots.title: The angler
spots.text: A figure in the reeds, with a rowboat pulled up just below. He is painted with a handful of dark strokes and can pass for part of the bank.

spots.title: The far meadow
spots.text: Those pale specks on the sunlit grass are haymakers. This is where the wagon is going. The whole picture is one short trip to work.

lesson.text: Why is a wagon standing in a river at all? The stream is shallow here, a ford, and the crossing leads to the meadows. People have also suggested the men paused to cool the horses and to wet the wooden wheels, which shrink in hot weather and work loose from their iron rims.

The house on the left was real, and it is still standing. It was rented by a farmer named Willy Lott, a neighbor of the Constables. The painter's father owned Flatford Mill, just out of view behind us. Constable grew up within a short walk of every tree in this picture.
According to Constable's first biographer, Willy Lott was born in that house and lived there for more than eighty years, spending only four nights of his whole life away from it.
Everything so far looks toward the cart. One small witness on the near bank does the same job for you, and Constable placed him there on purpose.
Somebody on the near bank is watching the wagon go by. Can you spot him?

spots.title: The dog
spots.text: A brown and white dog, head turned toward the wagon. His glance points yours in the same direction. A horse and rider once stood near here, then a barrel. Constable painted both out.

lesson.text: A dog, a cart, a cottage. In 1821 that was a problem. Serious painting meant ancient history, the Bible, or at least an Italian-looking view with ruins. A wet corner of Suffolk at lunchtime was not considered a subject. Constable even titled it “Landscape: Noon,” as if the hour of the day were the real topic.
The picture feels casual, like a glance. It is carefully built.

lines.label: A low horizon
lines.text: On the right the land stops less than two fifths of the way up. Everything above is weather. Constable said the sky should be the chief “organ of sentiment,” the part that carries the feeling.

lines.label: The dark mass
lines.text: House and trees form one big block of shade on the left. It works like a stage curtain pulled half aside, so the sunlit meadow on the right looks brighter still.

lines.label: Dog, wagon, meadow
lines.text: From the dog to the wagon to the haymakers, one diagonal carries you out of the shade and into the sun. It is the wagon's own route.

lesson.text: That sky is not decoration. Bright piled clouds on the right, a gray bank sliding in from the left: the light on the field is about to change. In the very months around this painting, Constable was on Hampstead Heath painting clouds alone, noting the date, the hour and the wind on the back of each study.
Constable dabbed tiny flecks of pure white over water and leaves to make them sparkle like wet things in sunlight. Critics hated it and nicknamed the effect “Constable's snow.”

The Academy crowd admired the painting and nobody bought it. Three years later a Paris dealer, John Arrowsmith, took it to France with two other works. At the Paris Salon of 1824, the French state exhibition, it caused a stir, and King Charles X awarded Constable a gold medal.

French painters were startled by how fresh it looked: broken touches of different greens instead of one smooth brown-green, light that seemed to move. The young Eugène Delacroix later said that seeing Constable's pictures made him rework part of his own large painting for that Salon. Constable himself never went to Paris. He never left England in his life.
Constable proved that a place you know by heart, painted at the scale of a history picture, can carry as much feeling as any battle or myth.

spots.title: Willy Lott's house
spots.text: Red roof tiles, a chimney, a small window. The building survives at Flatford in Suffolk and is still recognizable from this angle.

spots.title: Noon clouds
spots.text: Fair-weather clouds, heaped and bright on top with flat gray bases. They are lit from high above, which is how you know the hour.

spots.title: The gray bank
spots.text: A darker, heavier cloud drifts over the trees. Sun and threat share one sky, as they usually do in an English summer.

spots.title: Broken water
spots.text: The stream is made of short, separate strokes: brown, olive, slate, then quick pale touches on top. Up close it is rough. From a few steps back it shines.

spots.title: Red harness
spots.text: A few spots of red on the horses' collars. Small as they are, they pull your eye straight to the center of a picture made mostly of green and brown.

spots.title: The lone tree
spots.text: A slim tree stands apart from the dark group, catching full sun. It marks the hinge between the shaded half of the picture and the open one.

lesson.text: The painting's fame has made it a target. In 2013 a protester stuck a photograph onto the canvas, and in 2022 climate activists taped their own version of the scene over it and glued their hands to the frame.

quiz.question: Why did Constable paint The Hay Wain about six feet wide?
options: So it would stand out on the crowded walls of the Royal Academy exhibition
Because a French collector ordered that size
To fit the wall of his father's mill
quiz.explanation: Small landscapes got lost among hundreds of pictures hung frame to frame, so he scaled up.

quiz.question: Where was the picture actually painted?
options: Outdoors on the bank of the Stour
In his London house, from earlier sketches
quiz.explanation: He worked in London during the winter, using drawings and oil studies made in Suffolk.

quiz.question: What does the wagon in the painting carry?
options: Nothing: it is on its way to the meadow
quiz.explanation: The wain is empty and heading toward the haymakers in the far field.

quiz.question: What did critics call “Constable's snow”?
options: The pale walls of the cottage
The white flecks he used to make water and leaves sparkle
quiz.explanation: The nickname mocked his tiny dabs of pure white.

quiz.question: What happened when the painting was shown in Paris in 1824?
options: The king of France awarded Constable a gold medal
It was refused by the jury
quiz.explanation: Charles X gave him a gold medal at the Salon, though Constable never traveled to receive it in person.

quiz.question: Under what title did Constable first exhibit it?
quiz.explanation: The hour of the day was his stated subject; the famous title came later.

facts.text: Constable painted The Hay Wain on the riverbank in front of the scene.
facts.explanation: He painted it in London from sketches made in Suffolk years before.

facts.text: Before the final canvas, Constable painted a full-size oil sketch of the whole composition.
facts.explanation: The six-foot sketch survives in the Victoria and Albert Museum.

facts.text: The painting sold immediately at the Royal Academy in 1821.
facts.explanation: It found no buyer in London and went to a Paris dealer three years later.
